raw_response:
I'm a 53-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with an education background in agriculture. I've got 12 mu of land and a family of four. Let me think through my plan for this year.

I've been farming this land for 40 years, so I know every corner of it. My 12 mu isn't big, but it's what I have. With my agricultural education, I understand the science — nitrogen use efficiency, critical growth stages, water requirements — but I'm also cash-constrained. I can't just throw money at the problem. Every yuan I spend on inputs has to come back in yield.

**Winter wheat** — I plant in mid-October, around the 12th to 15th. I use an improved semi-dwarf variety, Jinmai 47 or something similar. For fertilizer, I target about 18 kg N per mu total — 10 kg as base fertilizer (compound fertilizer with some P and K), then 8 kg urea at jointing stage around late March. I won't go higher because the marginal return drops off, and I need cash for the maize season too. I'll irrigate four times: once before winter freeze-up, once at green-up in early spring, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The pumping costs about 25-30 yuan per mu per irrigation, so that's nearly 120 yuan per mu just for water, but wheat without irrigation in Quzhou is gambling.

**Summer maize** — This is the tough one. After wheat harvest in early June, I've got maybe 5-7 days to get the maize in the ground. I hire a custom combine for wheat harvest — costs about 50 yuan per mu — and then I plant maize immediately, around June 10th-12th. I use hybrid seed, bought fresh each year. Saved seed from hybrids is unpredictable. For fertilizer, I put down 16 kg N per mu as a one-time base application at planting — there's no time for tillage between crops, so I broadcast and incorporate lightly, or I use a no-till planter if I can rent one. If the season looks dry, I'll irrigate twice: once right after planting to ensure emergence, and once at the big flare stage in August. Maize yield on my land has been around 500 kg per mu in good years, maybe 450 in dry ones.

**Pesticides** — For wheat, I spray a herbicide in early spring if I see too much weeds. For maize, I usually apply a pre-emergence herbicide right after planting, and maybe an insecticide if aphids show up. I don't spray prophylactically — I scout first. That saves money.

**Labor** — My wife and I do most of the work. My son works in the county town but comes back for harvest and planting. My daughter-in-law helps with pesticide spraying and weeding. I might hire 2-3 days of labor for the maize planting rush if the weather window is tight. Family labor is about 25 days total across both crops, hired labor maybe 3 days.

**Budget tradeoffs** — I'm spending about 850-900 yuan per mu on inputs for the whole double-crop system. That feels tight but necessary. I could save 100 yuan by cutting one irrigation or reducing fertilizer, but with my education I know that would cost me 50-80 kg of yield per mu, and at 2.4 yuan per kg for wheat and 2.2 for maize, that's not worth it. I keep a small cash reserve — about 1,500 yuan — for emergencies.
